*Tomas stops a respectful distance off and plants his staff.*

"There it is. They came out of that dark stand—" *he nods at the trees, a dense fold of alder and old oak shading a hollow below* "—took her, and went back the same way. That hollow runs up into the high woods for miles. Nobody goes in there much."

*He looks at the sky, then at Alaric.*

"I'll leave you to it, then. Rain's an hour off, maybe two. When you're done out here, come down to the mill—someone will always be there." *He hesitates at the fence gap.* "One thing. *Tomas doesn't argue. He taps the stick once against his boot, looks at the sky, then at the boy with the sword, and nods.*

"Don't die up here, then. Millbrook's the low ground if you need us."

*He goes back down the sheep trail, and the rain takes his footsteps.*

*The trail runs north through the alders and into the pines. It isn't hard to follow—the drag marks keep reappearing where the ground softens, wool on bark, a hind print pressed deep beside a smaller one—and as Alaric climbs, the rain starts working for him too: the woods go quiet, birds down to nothing, and the wolves' sign stays fresh-looking under the wet. Forty minutes in he crosses where they rested, flattened bracken in a dry hollow under a leaning pine, and the prints leave it in a lope—moving, but not hurrying. Half a mile further, the drag marks end. Blood on a rock, cracked bone, wool worked into the needles. They fed here a second time.*

*Beyond that point the trail changes. The prints fan out—a third set, lighter, then a fourth, small, and the ground is crossed and recrossed with runs packed hard by repeated use. A game trail gone wolf-wide, worn into the slope like a road. Scat at intervals along it, old and new. This is their regular ground now, not a route to somewhere else.*

*Up through the pines, maybe two hundred yards off, there's a smell of musk and old kill on the wind, and a dark break in the tree line where the slope shelves back under a granite outcrop—likely where the trail leads. Nothing is moving in sight yet. The rain comes down steadier, dripping off the pine needles, and the woods hold still around him.*

*Steel rings out of the scabbard and the rain carries the sound down the slope.*

*The bitch's head snaps toward him. No growl at first—just stillness, ears forward, weighing the two-legged thing coming down open ground with a blade in its hand. Then her lip peels back and a low sound rolls out of her chest, deep enough to feel through the wet needles underfoot. The yearling wakes at it, scrambles up, and circles behind her with its hackles a ridge of dark fur.*

*She doesn't run and doesn't hide. She drops her head, tail level and stiff, and starts forward up the slope—angled, cutting sideways toward Alaric's flank, trying to put him between herself and the ravine where her den is. The yearling spreads the other way, wider, its whining high and thin. Two lines of approach, closing like a closing pair of jaws.*

*Twenty yards. Fifteen. Rain runs off the blade in Alaric's fist. The bitch's muscles bunch, and both wolves commit at once—the yearling darting in fast toward his left side, all noise and teeth, while the big bitch drives straight up the slope at him, silent now, jaws opening.*

deltas.note: marshmint grows in patches near the boundary stakes; a full basket is required

gen.prose:
"Herb Run too? Busy day." She logs it beneath the escort entry. "Full basket, mind — not a hatful. Marshmint's the stuff with the square stem and the blunt purple heads; smell it and you'll know. Don't wander into the deep reeds past the boundary stakes. That's not Guild rules, that's just sense."

The rain has thinned to a drizzle by the time he's out the Guildhall door. Grainmarket Row runs downhill toward the mill, the leat glinting along the cobbles in a channel cut for grain barges. Past Harrow's yard the ground turns soft — cart ruts filling with water, the smell of wet chaff giving way to mud and rotting reeds.

The reedbeds spread east of the leat across a low, sopping flat, gold-grey stalks taller than a man, hissing under the drizzle. Wooden stakes with faded red paint mark where the safe ground ends, maybe forty paces out into the reeds. Closer in, on the tussocks and the muddy shelves near the waterline, low green patches grow — square-stemmed, and when a boot presses near one, the smell comes up sharp and cool.

Frogs go quiet as he wades in over the first tussocks. Water seeps through stitching within a dozen steps; the mud pulls at each footfall. Somewhere out in the deeper reeds, well past the stakes, something heavy shifts — a slow push of stalks parting, then closing, then nothing. Herons hunt these flats, by the look of the tracks stitched through the mud, webbed and three-toed, some as long as a hand.

The nearest mint patches sit an easy reach from the stakes, plenty of them, leaves beaded with rain.

deltas.s: reedbeds east of the mill leat
deltas.o: along the path's reach; dense clumps remain farther out in the wet

gen.prose:
The first armful is easy — clumps within reach of the path, stems snapping clean under his thumb, cold water wicking up his sleeves. He lays the pile on the dry crest of the drainage path and goes back for more.

By the third trip the mud has found its way through every seam of his boots. The beds repeat themselves: tussock, waterline, mint, reed. The beaten trail stays where it is, out toward open water, and nothing comes up it while he works. Once, mid-crouch on a hummock, the water a hand's width from slopping over his boot tops, something small dives off a reed stem and is gone — a water rat or nothing worth naming.

The rhythm settles. Snap, strip the coarse lower leaves, lay them one way. The smell of crushed mint builds until it coats the inside of his nose, sharp enough to taste. His back learns the stoop. Out on the leat the millrace keeps up its one note, and the mist burns off toward noon, leaving a pale, working sort of sky.

By late afternoon the pile on the path is a genuine heap — two, three armfuls' worth, more than any basket he has seen at the Guild board would hold. Bundling it is its own problem: he ends up twisting long reed stems into crude ties around three tight sheaves, mint bundled like wheat, heavy and dripping. The weight of it rides hard on his arms for the walk back, and his shoulders will remember the day tomorrow, the day he also has a cart to stand beside at first light.

The light is going gold and long over the reeds when he straightens for the last time. The reedbeds are picked over along the path's reach; farther out, the good clumps sit deep in the wet, a job for waders or a colder morning. What he has is enough — more than enough, unless the Guild clerk weighs with a harsh hand.

The town's rooftops show dark against the sunset by the time the drainage path meets the cart track, and the Guildhall's windows are lit.

deltas.objective: deliver a full basket of marshmint to the Guild

gen.prose:
Hauling it is slower work than gathering. He makes two trips of it — half the pile bundled in his arms and against his chest, mint smell soaking into his sleeves, the second load carried the same way — and each walk down the drainage path and back along the leat takes the best part of half an hour under the weight. His shoulders burn by the time Redmarch's walls rise out of the mist. The gate guards glance at the green mess he is carrying and lose interest.

The Guildhall is warmer than the road, hearth going, the after-work crowd thicker than the morning's — a couple of tables of off-duty soldiers, the mud-booted adventurer gone. He brings the marshmint to the counter and the clerk hefts the whole bundle onto the weigh-scale's pan with both hands, pushing the stems down.

"Marshmint, whole and clean, not stripped." The needle settles. "That'll pass." She marks the Herb Run slip, stamps it, and counts four copper pieces onto the counter — the full basket rate, barely. "Herb Run's done. Escort leaves at first light, don't forget."

The coins sit by his hand on the worn counter wood.

The desk clerk — a broad man with ink-stained fingers this time — takes the marked slip, counts coins across the counter from the payout box, and slides them over with the Guild's compliments. Three coppers' worth of wet mint, weighed and done.

Evening Redmarch is at its loudest. Lamps are being lit along Grainmarket Row, and the side streets off it run with the smell of woodsmoke and frying onions. He walks with the damp clothes clinging cold to his legs, past a farrier still hammering, past a shrine alcove where a woman leaves a candle burning, past two inns he can rule out by sound alone — one all rowdy singing, one silent and shuttered. The third, on a lane called Candlemakers' Row, sits between a chandler's and a cobbler's: a low timbered building with a boar's head carved over the door, the sign reading The Drowned Boar, steam-smell of stew leaking out when a man pushes in ahead of him.

Inside it is warm and half-full — carters, a pair of off-duty watchmen by the window, an old dog by the hearth. The woman behind the bar is grey-haired, sleeves rolled, wiping tankards. She looks him over — the mud, the bare chest where his shirt hangs as a sling, the rapier.

"Reedbeds, were it. Guild novice by the plate." She nods at it on his belt. "Room's four copper, bath's two, and I'll wash that kit overnight for a copper — you'll not wear it again till it's scrubbed anyway, you'll take a fever. Stew and bread's a copper." She sets the tankard rag down. "Well? Room and bath both, or are you sleeping in the reeds?"
